node.label: Karl Marx
node.date_label: 1848: Manifesto of the Communist Party (with Friedrich Engels) · 1859: A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy: preface · 1867: Capital I · 1877: Letter to the editorial board of Otechestvenniye Zapiski (writing)
node.description: A critic of political economy whose accounts of production, property and exploitation became resources for historical materialism. His writings contain strong developmental propositions alongside historically qualified arguments; these are preserved as claims to compare, rather than silently harmonized.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Manifesto of the Communist Party (with Friedrich Engels) (1848); A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy: preface (1859); Capital I (1867); Letter to the editorial board of Otechestvenniye Zapiski (writing) (1877).
node.scope_note: Selected theoretical contributions and dated texts, with original, revised, translated and posthumous forms distinguished. Source notes state actual reading extent; no complete monograph or comprehensive reception survey is claimed. Existing collective relationships and source/roster qualifications remain.

proposed_edges.relationship: Makes production relations, productive forces and the forms in which people fight conflicts central historical questions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 1859 preface core paragraphs read. Strong forces/relations propositions are Marx’s argument; the existing separately sourced 1877 rejection of a universal Western-European path remains in the group context.

proposed_edges.relationship: Criticizes colonial land restriction as a means of making people dependent on wage labour.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own Capital I chapter 33 opening and colonial-land discussion read. This is a specific criticism of Wakefield; Mill is not named in this passage, and no direct Marx-to-Mill attack or complete Indigenous history is inferred.
